name: Army Survival Manual
description: Field-tested survival skills from the U.S. Army survival manual FM 3-05.70: water, fire, shelter, food, signaling and navigation.

license.attribution: Source: U.S. Army Field Manual FM 3-05.70, Survival. A work of the U.S. federal government — public domain.

guides.title: Finding and purifying water
guides.summary: How to locate water in any environment, build solar stills, and purify unsafe water before drinking.
guides.body:
Water is one of your most urgent needs in a survival situation. You cannot live long without it, especially in hot areas where you lose water rapidly through perspiration. Even in cold areas you need a minimum of 2 liters per day to maintain efficiency. Heat, cold, stress and exertion all drain body fluid, so obtaining an adequate supply is one of your first goals.

# Finding water

- In dry country, dig in valleys and low areas, at the foot of concave banks of dry riverbeds, at the foot of cliffs or rock outcrops, and wherever you find damp surface sand or green vegetation.
- All trails lead to water. Follow the direction in which trails converge; droppings and trampled terrain mark the way. Birds circle over water holes and fly to water at dawn and dusk, fast and close to the ground.
- Heavy dew can provide water: tie rags or tufts of fine grass around your ankles and walk through dew-covered grass before sunrise, wringing the water into a container — up to 1 liter an hour is possible.
- Bees or ants entering a hole in a tree may point to a water-filled hole. Siphon it, scoop it, or stuff in cloth and wring it out.
- Rainwater caught in clean containers or in plants is usually safe to drink. Catch rain in tarps or other water-holding material.

## Water from plants

- Green bamboo thickets are an excellent source: bend a green stalk, tie it down, and cut off the top. Water drips freely through the night. Purify it first.
- Cut down a banana or plantain tree leaving a 30-centimeter stump and scoop out the center into a bowl. The first three fillings are bitter; later ones are palatable. Covered against insects, the stump supplies water up to 4 days.
- Cut a notch in a vine as high as you can reach, then cut the vine off close to the ground and catch the liquid. Bruise a lower palm frond and pull it down so the tree "bleeds," or smash moist pulpy roots and stalks and catch the liquid. Young green coconut water is a good thirst quencher; mature coconut milk contains a laxative oil, so drink in moderation only.

> ⚠️ Do not drink any plant liquid that is sticky, milky, or bitter tasting, and do not keep plant sap longer than 24 hours — it ferments and becomes dangerous.

## Solar stills

- Vegetation bag: half to three-quarters fill a clear plastic bag with green leafy vegetation (no sharp spines), add a small rock, tie the mouth tightly, and lay it mouth-downhill in full sunlight. Water condenses around the rock. This yields the most of the still types.
- Transpiration bag: tie a plastic bag airtight over a leafy tree limb with a tube inserted. The same limb works 3 to 5 days without harm.
- Belowground still: dig a bowl-shaped hole about 1 meter across and 60 centimeters deep in moist soil, set a container in a center sump, cover the hole with plastic sheet weighted at its apex over the container, and drink through a tube without opening it. If polluted or salty water is all you have, pour it into a trough dug just outside the lip; the soil filters it as the still draws it.
- A still needs about 24 hours to yield 0.5 to 1 liter. Plan on at least three stills for one person's daily needs.

> ⚠️ Never use poisonous vegetation in a still. It will produce poisonous liquid.

# Purifying water

1. Clear muddy, stagnant or foul-smelling water by letting it stand 12 hours or filtering it through layers of sand, crushed rock, charcoal and cloth. Filtering only clears water — you must still purify it.
2. Boil to a rolling boil: the safest method, destroying all living waterborne pathogens. Charcoal from your fire removes some odors and chemicals; let the water stand 45 minutes.
3. Use water purification tablets, following label directions exactly.
4. Use iodine: 5 drops of 2 percent tincture per liter of clear water, 10 drops if cloudy or cold, standing 30 minutes.
5. Use chlorine bleach: 2 drops of 5.25 percent sodium hypochlorite per liter, wait 30 minutes — 60 minutes if cold or cloudy. Bleach strength varies, so check the label.
6. Loosen the cap and upend the container so treated water rinses the threads where your mouth touches.

> ⚠️ Never drink seawater or urine and do not substitute alcohol — each pulls more fluid from your body than it adds. Seawater is about 4 percent salt; ridding the body of 1 liter of it consumes about 2 liters of your own water.

> ⚠️ Melt snow and ice before consuming it. Eating snow lowers body temperature and causes more dehydration. Gray or opaque sea ice is salty; only bluish, crystalline ice is low in salt.

# Waterborne threats

- Giardia causes explosive, watery diarrhea with severe cramps lasting 7 to 14 days.
- Cryptosporidium is similar but worse and prolonged; iodine and bleach are not fully effective against it. Only a rolling boil or a commercial microfilter or reverse-osmosis filter neutralizes it reliably.
- Dysentery, cholera, typhoid, hepatitis A, blood flukes and leeches also travel in untreated water, especially near settlements and in the tropics.

> ⚠️ When in doubt, purify all water you get from vegetation or from the ground.

guides.title: Firecraft: building and lighting fires
guides.summary: Site selection, tinder, kindling and fuel, four fire lays, and modern and primitive ignition methods.
guides.body:
The ability to start and keep a fire can make the difference between living and dying. Fire provides warmth, cooks and preserves food, purifies water, sterilizes bandages, signals for rescue, protects against animals, and lifts morale. It can also burn you, destroy equipment, start a wildfire, and cause carbon monoxide poisoning inside a shelter.

# How fire works

Fuel does not burn directly: heat turns fuel into gas, and the gas combined with oxygen burns. The fire triangle — **air, heat and fuel** — must stay in balance; remove any side and the fire goes out. The correct ratio comes only with practice.

# Site selection and preparation

1. Choose a dry spot sheltered from wind, near your shelter, with fuel available.
2. Clear a circle at least 1 meter (3 feet) across down to bare soil so the fire cannot spread.
3. If time allows, build a fire wall of logs or rocks to reflect heat where you want it, cut wind, and reduce sparks.
4. In deep snow, lay green logs side by side in layers, top layer crosswise, as a dry base.

> ⚠️ Do not use wet or porous rocks in a fire wall — they may explode when heated.

## Concealed and efficient fires

- Dakota fire hole: dig a hole, dig a ventilation hole on its upwind side, and build the fire in the hole. It conceals the flame, cooks well, and burns hot even in wind.

# Materials: tinder, kindling, fuel

- **Tinder** is absolutely dry material that ignites from a spark: birch bark, shredded inner bark of cedar, chestnut or red elm, fine wood shavings, dead grass, ferns, moss and fungi, straw, sawdust, dead evergreen needles, punk from rotted logs, bird down, down seed heads like milkweed and cattail, pocket lint, waxed paper, and charred cloth. Charred cloth — cotton heated black but not burned, kept airtight — holds a spark a long time; make it in advance and carry it in your kit.
- **Kindling** is readily combustible material added to burning tinder to raise the fire's temperature: small twigs, small strips of wood, dry standing wood and dead branches, split wood, and dry grasses twisted into bunches.
- **Fuel** burns slowly and steadily: dry standing wood, dry dead branches, the dry heart of fallen trunks and large branches, and green wood finely split. Gather tinder and kindling along the trail as you go.

# Fire lays

- **Tepee**: arrange tinder and a few sticks of kindling in a cone and light the center. Logs fall inward, feeding the fire; burns well even with wet wood.
- **Lean-to**: push a green stick into the ground at a 30-degree angle into the wind, place tinder deep under it, lean kindling against the stick, and light the tinder, adding kindling as it catches.
- **Cross-ditch**: scratch a cross about 30 centimeters (12 inches) across and 7.5 centimeters (3 inches) deep, put tinder in the middle, and build a kindling pyramid above. The shallow ditches sweep air under the tinder.
- **Pyramid**: lay two small logs parallel, then progressively smaller layers crosswise. Light a starter fire on top; it burns downward unattended through the night.

# Lighting the fire

1. Always light from the upwind side, with tinder, kindling and fuel laid to burn as long as you need.
2. Matches: keep waterproof, stored in a waterproof container with a dependable striker pad.
3. Convex lens: on bright sunny days only, focus sun through a lens from binoculars, a camera or a magnifying glass onto the tinder until it smolders, then gently blow it into flame.
4. Metal match or ferrocerium rod: rest a flat dry leaf under the tinder with an edge exposed, and scrape sparks onto it with a knife.
5. Battery: attach a wire to each terminal and touch the bare ends together next to the tinder so the spark ignites it.

## Primitive ignition

- **Flint and steel** is the easiest primitive method: strike flint or another hard, sharp-edged rock with carbon steel (stainless sparks poorly). When the tinder catches, blow until it flames.
- **Fire-plow**: cut a straight groove in a softwood base and plow the blunt tip of a hardwood shaft up and down it; friction ignites the wood particles.
- **Bow and drill**: use a socket (stone or hardwood with a depression), a seasoned hardwood drill about 2 by 25 centimeters (3/4 by 10 inches), a seasoned softwood fire board with a depression and a V-cut on the underside, and a green bow with tight cord. Saw the bow around the drill, held upright with the socket, until you have smooth motion — then press harder and work faster. Hot black powder grinds into tinder placed under the V-cut; blow until it ignites.

> ⚠️ Never burn charcoal or a smoldering fire inside an enclosed shelter without generous ventilation. Carbon monoxide kills quietly while you sleep.

> ⚠️ Dry damp wood near the fire, bank coals to keep them alive overnight, and be certain the fire is completely out before leaving camp. In dry country one escaped coal can start a wildfire.

guides.title: Survival shelters
guides.summary: Choosing a safe site and building lean-tos, debris huts, swamp beds, snow and desert shelters with minimal gear.
guides.body:
A shelter protects you from sun, insects, wind, rain, snow and temperature extremes, and it helps maintain your will to survive. In some areas shelter takes precedence over food and possibly even water: prolonged cold exposure causes exhaustion, and an exhausted person can lose the will to survive.

Your **primary shelter is your clothing**. Keep it dry, clean and layered loose enough to trap warm air. A common error is building the shelter too large: it must be big enough to protect you and small enough to contain your body heat, especially in cold climates.

# Choosing a site

Remember **BLISS**: Blend in with the surroundings, Low silhouette, Irregular shape, Small, Secluded location.

- The site must contain material for the shelter and be level enough to lie down on.
- It should protect against animals, falling rocks and dead trees, and be free of insects, reptiles and poisonous plants.
- Avoid flash flood areas in foothills, avalanche and rockslide paths, ground below any high-water mark, and low ground (ravines, creek beds) where cold air and insects collect at night.
- Seek natural shelters first — caves, crevices, thick bushes, depressions, leeward rocks, fallen trees — and alter them to save energy.

> ⚠️ Before using any natural formation, check for poisonous snakes, ticks, mites, scorpions and stinging ants, and look up for loose rocks, dead limbs and coconuts.

# Quick shelters from a poncho or tarp

- **Poncho lean-to**: tie off the hood, lash rope from the corner grommets of one long side waist-high between two trees 2 to 3 meters (7 to 10 feet) apart, and stake the free edge down with sharpened sticks. Tie short drip sticks near the grommets so rain runs down the rope, and angle the back into the wind. Add a center support line for more than one night.
- **Poncho tent**: tie ropes to the center grommets of each side, stretch the poncho tight between two trees at knee height, and stake both sides down — a low silhouette that protects two sides.
- Pile brush or your pack against open sides, and lay leaves or pine needles inside as floor insulation.

> ⚠️ At rest you can lose as much as 80 percent of your body heat into the ground. Always insulate between your body and the earth.

# Field-expedient lean-to

1. Tie a pole horizontally between two trees at waist to chest height (or a bipod of forked sticks).
2. Lay one end of several longer poles (beams) against the support, back of the shelter into the wind.
3. Crisscross saplings or vines across the beams.
4. Cover the frame with brush, leaves, needles or grass, shingling from the bottom up.
5. Lay bedding inside; pile brush at the entrance for a door.
6. In cold weather, build a fire reflector wall of stacked green logs between stake rows, packed with dirt, so it throws heat into the shelter and shields the fire.

## Variations for wet, warm and snowy country

- **Swamp bed**: in marsh or flooded ground, drive four poles (bamboo is ideal) firmly into the ground as a rectangle strong enough to hold you, secure two crosspoles above the water line, lay lengthwise poles across, cover with broad leaves, and build a small fire pad of drying mud in one corner.
- **Beach shade shelter**: above the high-water mark, dig a trench running north-south so it catches the least sun, wide enough to lie in; mound sand on three sides, roof the trench with driftwood, and line it with grass.
- **Desert shade**: stretch a tarp between a rock outcrop or sand mound and the ground; if material allows, double it with a 30 to 45 centimeter (12 to 18 inch) air gap between layers, which drops the temperature below.
- **Belowground desert shelter**: dig a trench 45 to 60 centimeters (18 to 24 inches) deep between dunes or rocks, pile the sand around three sides, and cover with material weighted down — reducing midday heat by 16 to 22 degrees C (30 to 40 degrees F).

> ⚠️ Digging a belowground desert shelter is heavy work that sweats out precious water. Build in the cool of morning or evening, never in the heat of the day.

# The debris hut: the warmest emergency shelter

1. Make a tripod with two short stakes and a long ridgepole, or rest the ridgepole on a sturdy base about waist height.
2. Prop large sticks along both sides as ribbing — wide enough for your body, steep enough to shed moisture.
3. Lay finer sticks and brush crosswise as a lattice that keeps insulation from falling through.
4. Pile light, dry, soft debris — leaves, grass, pine needles — at least 1 meter (about 3 feet) thick. Thicker is better.
5. Spread a 30-centimeter (1-foot) layer of insulation on the floor.
6. Pile insulation at the entrance to pull in after you, and shingle branches over the outside so storms cannot strip the debris.

## Snow country

- **Tree-pit snow shelter**: beneath a bushy evergreen, dig out the snow around the trunk, pack snow around the top and walls for support, and lay cut evergreen boughs over the pit and on the floor.

> ⚠️ Never light a fire inside a closed snow shelter or tightly sealed space without a vent — carbon monoxide from an oxygen-starved flame kills without warning.

guides.title: Food procurement: plants, animals and traps
guides.summary: Safe general guidance on insects, fish, game and simple traps, plus preparing and preserving wild food.
guides.body:
You can live for weeks without food, but endurance drops daily, so begin food gathering early — after water and shelter are secure. Concentrate on smaller animals: more abundant and easier to prepare. With few exceptions anything that crawls, swims, walks or flies can be eaten, but you must overcome aversion to unfamiliar food, and should thoroughly cook all food whenever possible.

> ⚠️ Unknown plants are a different matter: never eat any plant you have not positively identified. Watching what animals eat, boiling, or a plant's color do not reliably separate edible from deadly. See the poisonous plants guide first.

# Easiest animal foods first

- **Insects** are the most abundant, easily caught life form, and many are 65 to 80 percent protein. Look in rotting logs, under stones and boards, and in grassy fields. Avoid insects that sting or bite, hairy or brightly colored ones, caterpillars, pungent ones, spiders, and disease carriers such as ticks, flies and mosquitoes. Cook hard-shelled insects (beetles, grasshoppers) — they carry parasites — and remove wings and barbed legs.
- **Worms** are excellent protein. Dig in damp humus soil or watch after rain; drop them in clean water 15 minutes to purge, then eat.
- **Crustaceans and mollusks**: crayfish hide under stream stones by day and take offal bait on a string; shrimp come to a light at night; snails, clams and mussels gather in the shallows and in tidal pools. Steam, boil or bake shellfish in the shell, and cook all freshwater crustaceans, mollusks and fish.
- **Fish** are usually more abundant than mammals and can be taken silently. They feed heavily before a storm, go off the bite in muddy swollen water, and rest in eddies, deep pools, under overhanging brush and around submerged logs. Light attracts them at night.
- **Amphibians and reptiles**: frogs are good food; avoid toads, salamanders, brightly colored frogs and all tree frogs. Handle all reptiles as salmonella carriers — cook thoroughly and wash your hands fastidiously.
- **Birds** are all edible. Take roosting birds at night by hand, net across regular flyways between roost, water and feeding areas, and gather eggs — leaving two or three marked eggs so the bird keeps laying.
- **Mammals** are all edible, but every mammal bites in self-defense and any bite risks infection. A cornered animal or a mother with young is dangerous in proportion to its size.

> ⚠️ Do not eat mussels in tropical zones during summer, never eat fish or shellfish from water where a red tide occurred within 72 hours, and never eat shellfish not covered by water at high tide.

> ⚠️ Cooking does not destroy some toxins. Ciguatera comes from tropical marine fish — barracuda, jacks, mackerel, triggerfish, snapper, grouper — that fed on toxic algae; puffer and porcupine fish can be deadly. Avoid box and hawksbill turtles and polar bear or bearded seal liver (lethal vitamin A).

> ⚠️ Do not eat spoiled fish — sunken eyes, peculiar odor, suspicious color, dents that stay pressed, slimy body, peppery taste. It can cause sudden paralysis and vomiting within hours; induce vomiting if symptoms appear.

# Traps and snares

Well-placed traps catch more than active hunting. Know the species, build a proper trap, mask your scent, and leave no alarming signs.

1. Read the sign: runs and trails, tracks, droppings, chewed vegetation, dens, feeding and watering areas. A trail serves several species; a run is smaller and used by one. Set traps only where passage is proven.
2. Use channelization: build a funnel-shaped barrier from the trail sides toward the trap, narrowest at the trap, so the animal cannot turn aside.
3. Match the trap to the animal: a simple snare is a wire noose over a trail or den entrance anchored to a stake; a drag noose hangs from a crossmember so brush entangles the animal; a twitch-up snare uses a bent sapling to spring and hang the prey; a squirrel pole carries nooses along a pole leaned against a tree; figure 4 and Paiute deadfalls drop a weight on the prey.
4. Bait with something the animal knows but cannot find nearby — peanut butter and salt both work — and scatter bits around the trap so it loses caution.
5. Mask human scent with mud from rotting vegetation or by smoking trap parts; never build with freshly cut live vegetation, and assemble the trap away from the site.

> ⚠️ Check traps from behind and carry a stout club. A trapped animal is dangerous, and any bite can infect. Bottle-type traps are favorite hiding places for snakes.

# Fishing without tackle

- Improvise hooks from pins, needles, wire, thorns, bone or wood. A gorge is a sharp-ended stick baited lengthwise that the fish swallows — let it take it deep before setting.
- A stakeout is a baited line tied between two saplings in the shallows. A gill net of about 2.5 centimeter (1 inch) mesh, angled across a stream, works while you do other tasks.
- To spear fish in shallow water, move the point slowly toward the fish and impale it with a sudden push — aim below the fish, because refraction makes it appear higher. Never throw the spear.

# Preparing and preserving

1. Bleed, gut and clean game immediately; fish spoils fast — cut out the gills and blood vessels near the spine, and gut fish over 10 centimeters (4 inches) long.
2. Inspect any mammal's liver: smooth, wet, deep red or purple is good. Discard a diseased-looking liver; the muscle meat is usually still sound.
3. Boil meat with the skin on where possible to keep fats and juices; boil scavenger birds at least 20 minutes to kill parasites.
4. Smoke strips no more than 6 millimeters (1/4 inch) thick over smoldering hardwood under an enclosure — smoke and gentle heat, not flame. Overnight smoking keeps meat about a week; two days preserves it 2 to 4 weeks.
5. Dry 6-millimeter strips with the grain in sun and moving air, covered against blowflies, until crisp and no longer cool to the touch.

> ⚠️ When cleaning a snake, cut off the head with 10 to 15 centimeters (4 to 6 inches) behind it to remove the venom sac, and bury the head.

guides.title: Signaling techniques
guides.summary: Fires, smoke, mirrors, ground symbols and audio signals that get a rescuer's attention and carry a message.
guides.body:
You must first get your rescuer's attention, and second send a message the rescuer understands. Attention-getters are things nature does not produce: straight lines, circles, triangles and X shapes in open areas, a large fire or flash of light, a large bright object moving slowly, and strong contrast of color or shadow. Know your signaling gear and be ready to use it on short notice — practice before you need it.

Pick signaling ground carefully: the largest available clear, flat area on the highest terrain, visible from the air.

# The rule of threes

Nature almost never repeats anything in groups of three, so **things in threes** read as man-made distress: three fires, three smoke columns, three whistle blasts, three flashes, three gunshots at distinct intervals.

# Visual signals

- **Fire** is the primary night signal. Build three fires in a triangle — the international distress signal — or in a line about 25 meters (83 feet) apart. If alone, keep one strong signal fire going. A hot coal bed can be detected by aircraft with infrared sensors after the flames die.
- **Smoke** is the primary day signal: three columns. Smother a large fire with green leaves, moss or a little water for white smoke; add rubber or oil-soaked rags for black smoke. Choose the color that contrasts with the background. Smoke works only on calm, clear days — wind, rain and snow disperse it.
- A **burning tree** (tree torch) draws attention: ignite a pitch-bearing evergreen by stacking dry wood in the lower branches, then add cut green trees for more smoke.

> ⚠️ Select an isolated tree for a tree torch and clear dry vegetation around any signal fire so you do not start a wildfire that endangers you.

- **Signal mirror**: on a sunny day your best device — polish a canteen cup or belt buckle if you have no mirror. To aim, catch the reflection on your palm or in the V between two raised fingers, bring it just below the aircraft until the craft sits in the V with the glare on your palm, then flash rhythmically onto your aim point. Sweep the horizon even seeing nothing: pilots have reported flashes up to 160 kilometers (about 96 miles) away.

> ⚠️ Do not flash a mirror rapidly — a pilot may mistake it for gunfire — and never hold the beam on a cockpit for more than a few seconds; it can blind the pilot. In haze, get high and flash toward the aircraft noise.

- **Flashlight or strobe** at night to send an SOS toward aircraft. Wear the mirror on a cord, glass side against your body.
- **Bright cloth**: lay out orange or violet material, flashing it to catch the eye; spread clothing on the ground or in treetops in a large geometric pattern that contrasts with the surroundings.
- **Natural material**: build shadow-casting mounds from brush, rocks, foliage or snow blocks. In snow, tramp letters and fill them with twigs; in sand, use boulders, vegetation or seaweed; in brush, cut patterns or sear the ground; in tundra, dig trenches or turn the sod.

# Ground-to-air emergency code

Make each symbol at least 4 meters (13 feet) wide and 6 meters (20 feet) long, keeping the 2:3 ratio if enlarged, with limbs 1 meter (3 feet) wide, contrasting strongly with the ground, in an open area, oriented north-south to catch the sun's shadow.

- **V** — require assistance
- **X** — require medical assistance
- **N** — no or negative
- **Y** — yes or affirmative
- A solid **arrow** — proceed in this direction

Straight lines, square corners and sharp angles do not occur in nature — that is what makes these symbols readable from the air.

# Audio signals and codes

- **Whistles** carry up to 1.6 kilometers (3/4 mile) — far louder than a human whistle. Three blasts at intervals signal distress.
- **Gunshots**: three shots at distinct intervals read as distress.
- **Radio** is the surest link: transmit from clear, unobstructed ground (radios are line-of-sight), keep the antenna at right angles to the aircraft and clear of your body and foliage, and conserve batteries — keep them warm in cold, out of extreme heat.
- **SOS** is three dots, three dashes, three dots — short and long pulses — by light, flag or whistle, repeated continuously.
- On water or snow, sea dye markers spread a slick visible for miles; use them only when you hear or sight an aircraft.

# When the aircraft responds

- Message received and understood: the aircraft rocks from side to side (day) or flashes green light (night).
- Received but not understood: a complete right-hand circle, or red flashes at night.
- Keep signaling and follow the aircrew's guidance until actually recovered — initial contact is not rescue.

guides.title: Direction finding and land travel
guides.summary: Finding north and south with shadows, a watch, the moon and stars, improvising a compass, and travel judgment.
guides.body:
You are fortunate in a survival situation if you have a map and compass — proficiency with them is worth learning beforehand. Without them, the sun and stars give a general direction, and knowledge of the terrain — ridgelines, rivers, coastlines, landmarks — turns a rough bearing into a usable course.

# The shadow-tip method

Simple, accurate, and valid everywhere on earth.

1. Stand a straight stick about 1 meter (3 feet) long upright on level ground where it casts a definite shadow. Mark the shadow tip with a stone or twig. This first mark is always **west**.
2. Wait 10 to 15 minutes for the shadow tip to move. Mark the new position — **east**.
3. Draw a straight line through the two marks: an approximate east-west line.
4. Stand with the first (west) mark on your left and the second (east) mark on your right: you are facing **north**.

- Slower but more accurate: in the morning, use a string tied to the stick to draw a clean arc through the first shadow mark. The shadow shrinks to nothing at midday, then lengthens; mark where it recrosses the arc in the afternoon. The line through both marks is an accurate east-west line.

# The watch method

Use an analog watch, or draw a clock face on paper or the ground set to the current time, on true local time without daylight saving.

- Northern Hemisphere: hold the watch horizontal, point the hour hand at the sun, and bisect the angle between the hour hand and 12 o'clock for a north-south line.
- Southern Hemisphere: point the 12 o'clock mark at the sun; the midpoint between 12 and the hour hand gives the north-south line.
- If unsure which end is north, remember the sun rises east, is due south at noon (Northern Hemisphere), and sits west after noon. On daylight saving time, bisect between the hour hand and 1 o'clock.
- The farther from the equator, the more accurate this method is.

# Using the moon

- If the moon rises before sunset, the illuminated side is to the **west**.
- If it rises after midnight, the illuminated side is to the **east** — a rough east-west reference through the night.

# Using the stars

- **Northern Hemisphere**: learn the Big Dipper (Ursa Major) and Cassiopeia, the "Lazy W." They rotate counterclockwise around opposite sides of the nearly stationary North Star, Polaris. Extend the Big Dipper's two pointer stars — the outer lip of the bowl — about five times their separation to find Polaris. With Cassiopeia, bisect the angle of the lazy (flattened) side of the W and extend about five times the W's height. Using both prevents mix-ups, since the Little Dipper's stars are dim. Polaris also sits about your latitude in degrees above a flat horizon — at 35 degrees north, scan 35 degrees up.
- **Southern Hemisphere**: no bright pole star exists; use the Southern Cross (Crux). Extend its long axis four and one-half to five times toward the horizon to find due south. The two bright pointer stars beside the Cross confirm the true Cross against the False Cross; the starless coal sac between them sits near south. From a fixed camp, drive stakes at night pointing at that ground spot to mark south by day.

# Improvised compasses

- Magnetize a needle-shaped piece of ferrous metal or a razor blade by stroking it slowly in one direction only with silk, through your hair, or with a magnet. Suspend it from a thread, or float it on water on wood, cork or a leaf, and it swings to a north-south line.
- With a battery of at least 2 volts and insulated wire in a coil touching the terminals, repeatedly insert one end of the metal into the coil to magnetize it.

# Other direction clues

- The moss-on-the-north-side-of-trees saying is **not** reliable — moss grows all around many trees.
- On stumps, annual rings grow wider on the side toward the equator, tighter toward the poles.
- In the Northern Hemisphere, south-facing slopes get more sun and lusher growth; north-facing slopes are cooler and damper and hold snow patches longer into summer. All effects reverse in the Southern Hemisphere.
- Prevailing winds help only if you know which way they normally blow in that region.

# Deciding whether to travel

- Stay with your shelter, vehicle and signals when rescue is likely and water is nearby: a stationary survivor with a signal is easier to find than a moving one.
- If you must move, fix direction by two independent methods, then follow terrain handrails that cannot be missed — a river, ridgeline, coastline, road — and note your back bearing so you can return.
- Travel in daylight, rest briefly every hour, and pace yourself: exhaustion causes judgment errors no skill can offset.
- Mark your route as you go, and stop at dusk to build shelter and signal while light remains.

guides.title: Survival medicine: self-aid fundamentals
guides.summary: Hygiene, dehydration, the ABCs of first aid, bleeding control, shock, wounds, bites and cold or heat injuries.
guides.body:
Medical problems compromise survival more than almost anything else, and without qualified help it is you who must know what to do. The ability to treat yourself sustains both health and morale. Survival medicine rests on prevention first: water, food, and high personal hygiene.

# Prevention: water, hygiene, feet

- The average adult must replace 2 to 3 liters of water daily at moderate exertion; heat, cold, intense activity, altitude, burns and illness raise the loss. Drink small amounts at regular intervals every hour — by the time you feel thirsty you are already 2 percent dehydrated, and repaying a deficit in the field is very hard.
- A 5 percent fluid loss brings thirst, irritability, nausea and weakness; 10 percent brings dizziness, headache, inability to walk, tingling limbs; 15 percent brings dim vision, painful urination, swollen tongue and numb skin. Beyond 15 percent can be fatal. Conserve **sweat, not water**: limit sweat-producing activity but keep drinking.
- Watch for dark strong-smelling urine, low urine output, sunken eyes, fatigue, loss of skin elasticity and a trench down the center of the tongue.
- Keep clean: wash hands after handling anything germ-laden and before food or water; bathe with a cloth and soapy water — feet, armpits, crotch, hands and hair. If water is scarce, take an air bath in sun and moving air for an hour, avoiding sunburn. Make soap from animal fat and wood-ash lye if possible.
- Care for feet daily: wash, dry, massage; keep toenails trimmed straight; check for blisters. Do not open a small blister — pad around it. If one must drain, run a sterilized needle and thread through it and leave the thread hanging out.
- Clean teeth daily with a chewed twig, cloth strip, or small amounts of salt or baking soda. Rest at least 10 minutes every hour of effort.

# Lifesaving steps: airway, bleeding, shock

1. **Airway**: if the person can cough or speak, let them clear the obstruction and stand by; if fully obstructed, give abdominal thrusts. Sweep the mouth clear, then open the airway with the jaw thrust — grasp the angles of the lower jaw and lift with both hands, elbows braced on the ground.
2. **Breathing**: pinch the nose and blow two complete breaths; look for the chest to rise, listen and feel for escaping air. If breathing does not resume, continue mouth-to-mouth, checking for vomit. CPR may be needed once bleeding is controlled — learn it beforehand.
3. **Bleeding**: arterial blood spurts bright red with the heartbeat and is most dangerous; venous blood flows steady and dark. Press directly on the wound, firmly and continuously. If bleeding persists after 30 minutes, apply a pressure dressing — a thick pad bound tightly over the wound — and do not remove it even when soaked. Raise the limb above heart level (except snakebite). If that fails, press the pressure point above the wound at a joint. Use a tourniquet only when all else has failed.
4. **Shock**: anticipate it in every injured person. Lay a conscious victim level with legs elevated 15 to 20 centimeters (6 to 8 inches); lay an unconscious victim on the side, head turned. Insulate from the ground, swap wet clothes for dry, improvise shelter, apply external warmth, and give small sips of warm salted or sugared fluid only if conscious — never to an unconscious victim or one with abdominal wounds. Rest at least 24 hours.

> ⚠️ Losing 1 liter of blood produces moderate shock, 2 liters severe shock, 3 liters is usually fatal. Control serious bleeding immediately — a victim can die within minutes.

> ⚠️ Use a tourniquet only as a last resort. Place it 5 to 10 centimeters (2 to 4 inches) above the wound — never on the wound, a joint, or the neck. A lone survivor does not loosen it once applied; if with others, release pressure briefly every 10 to 15 minutes to limit tissue death.

# Wounds

- Clean a wound at once: cut clothing away, look for an exit wound, and rinse — do not scrub — with large amounts of water under pressure.
- Use open treatment: do not suture or close a field wound. Leave it open to drain; a draining wound generally will not become life-threatening, however unpleasant it looks.
- Cover with a clean dressing, change it daily, and watch for infection: pain, swelling, redness, heat, pus.
- An infected wound needs warm moist compresses 30 minutes at a stretch, three or four times daily, gentle probing drainage, a fresh dressing, and plenty of water to drink.

# Bites and stings

- **Bee and wasp**: scrape the stinger and venom sac free with a fingernail or blade — never squeeze. Wash the site. If you are allergic, carry an insect sting kit; without antihistamine, a sting allergy in the field is life-threatening.
- **Spiders and scorpions**: know the black widow (red hourglass), the brown recluse (violin mark, ulcerating bite), the Australian funnelweb, and scorpions. Clean and dress the site, treat for shock, and be ready to maintain breathing. Check boots, bedding, clothing and shelter every morning; turn rocks and logs with a stick.
- **Ticks**: cover an attached tick with petroleum jelly, heavy oil or sap to cut its air, then grasp the mouthparts and pull the whole tick free without crushing it. Transmission generally needs 6 or more hours of attachment — inspect your body at least daily.
- **Snakebite**: reassure the victim and keep them still; remove rings, watches and anything constricting; clean the bite; keep the limb lower than the heart; place a lightly constricting band between wound and heart; immobilize the site; use mechanical suction if available. Envenomation shows as puncture marks, rapid painful swelling, spontaneous bleeding and — for neurotoxic venom — weakness and breathing difficulty within 2 hours.

> ⚠️ Do not give alcohol or tobacco to a snakebite victim, do not make deep cuts at the bite, do not put your hands on your face or rub your eyes, and do not break the blisters that form around the bite.

# Environmental injuries

- **Heatstroke**: swollen beet-red face, red eyes, no sweating, delirium or unconsciousness. Cool immediately — immerse in cool water, or douse and apply cool wet compresses to neck, armpits and crotch, wetting the head. Watch for relapse within 48 hours; treat dehydration with lightly salted water.
- **Hypothermia**: get the victim out of wind and wet into dry clothing and the best shelter, give warm fluids, and rewarm with skin-to-skin contact in a sleeping bag. Immediate treatment is the key.
- **Frostbite**: firm, pale, frozen tissue. Rewarm in water 37 to 42 degrees C (99 to 109 degrees F) — never rub it or hold it to open flame — then dry it and hold it against warm skin.
- **Trench foot**: days of damp cold. Keep feet dry; carry extra socks in a waterproof packet; dry wet socks against your body.
- **Diarrhea**: drink strong tea every 2 hours — its tannic acid helps control it — and if available 2 tablespoons of a ground chalk or charcoal and citrus-rind mixture every 2 hours.

> ⚠️ Use herbal and improvised remedies with extreme care, and only when you lack or have limited medical supplies. Some are dangerous and can cause further harm.

guides.title: Poisonous plants and dangerous animals
guides.summary: Identification-level guidance on toxic plants, snakes, spiders, and hazardous creatures on land and in the water.
guides.body:
Successful use of plants in a survival situation depends on positive identification, and knowing poisonous plants is as important as knowing edible ones. The same holds for animals: the threat from animals is less than from other parts of the environment, but smaller creatures — venomous snakes, spiders, insects — present far more danger than large predators, because you meet them unawares.

# How plants poison

- **Contact** — touching the plant irritates skin (dermatitis).
- **Ingestion** — eating any part of a poisonous plant.
- **Absorption or inhalation** — toxin taken through skin or breathed in, including smoke from burning poisonous plants.

Toxicity varies with growing conditions, subspecies and the person exposed, so there is no single rule for spotting a poisonous plant. Dismiss the myths: animals eating a plant safely does not make it safe for you; boiling removes many poisons but not all; red coloration marks some poisonous plants but many safe ones too.

> ⚠️ Avoid all mushrooms. Identification must be precise, some kill quickly, and some have no known antidote.

## Plants that trap the unwary

- Many poisonous plants mimic edible relatives: poison hemlock closely resembles wild carrot.
- Some are safe only in season or stage: pokeweed leaves are edible only in early growth; only the ripe May apple fruit is edible; black cherry foliage turns toxic as it wilts; jack-in-the-pulpit corms are poisonous unless sliced thin and dried for months. Potato tubers and tomato fruit are safe, but the green parts of both plants are poisonous.
- **Contact dermatitis** plants: poison ivy, poison oak, poison sumac, cowhage, the rengas tree and trumpet vine. Their irritant oil rides on skin, clothing and equipment, and acts faster when you are hot and sweating. If exposed, wash with soap and cold water at once; without water, wipe the skin repeatedly with dirt or sand — never over blisters.

> ⚠️ Never burn a contact-poisonous plant: the smoke carries the irritant into lungs and eyes.

- Plants that poison if **eaten** include castor bean, chinaberry, death camas, lantana, manchineel, oleander, pangi, physic nut, poison and water hemlocks, rosary pea and the strychnine tree. If you suspect ingestion, remove material from the mouth, induce vomiting in a conscious victim (warm saltwater or tickling the back of the throat), and dilute the poison with large quantities of water or milk. Keep a log of everything eaten.

# Dangerous animals

## On land

- **Snakes**: there are no infallible field rules for identifying venomous snakes — leave all snakes alone. Walk carefully and watch where you step; step **onto** logs and rocks rather than over them; look closely when picking fruit or working near water; turn logs and rocks with a stick; wear proper footgear, especially at night; check bedding, clothing and shelter before use. Do not tease or corner a snake — mambas, cobras and bushmasters attack when cornered, and closed eyes tell you nothing about whether it sleeps. Snake-free regions: New Zealand, Ireland, Cuba, Haiti, Jamaica, Puerto Rico, Polynesia, Hawaii and the polar regions.
- **Scorpions** haunt deserts, jungles and warm forests and are mostly nocturnal. Fatalities are rare but real for children, the elderly and the ill. Shake out boots, clothing and bedding every morning.
- **Spiders**: learn the brown recluse or fiddleback (violin mark; ulcerating bite), the widow family (dark bodies, hourglass markings; neurotoxic), the Australian funnelweb (large, aggressive at night), and tarantulas (painful, infection-prone bites; a few venomous species).
- **Bees, wasps and hornets**: most people recover in hours, but an allergic person can go into anaphylactic shock and die. Watch flowers and fruit where bees feed, beware meat-eating yellow jackets when cleaning fish or game; honeybees sting once and die, wasps and hornets repeatedly.
- **Ticks** carry Lyme disease, Rocky Mountain spotted fever and encephalitis; inspect daily, since roughly 6 hours of attachment is generally needed to transmit disease. Use repellent and tuck trousers into boots — the same habit deters **leeches**, which infest swamps and tropical waters and can enter nose and throat through untreated drinking water.
- **Bats**: treat every bat as a rabies risk and never handle one; the greater hazard is inhaling dust from dried bat guano in caves.
- **Lizards**: the Gila monster of the American Southwest and Mexico and the Mexican beaded lizard are the two venomous lizards — dark beaded skin, docile unless molested.
- **Large mammals**: avoid bears, lions and big grazing animals, move carefully through their ground, and never leave food around camp — it attracts predators.

## In rivers, bays and seas

- **Rivers**: electric eels (South America, up to 500 volts); piranhas, drawn to blood, most dangerous in shallow water in the dry season; snapping and soft-shelled turtles that amputate fingers; the male platypus of Australia, with poisonous hind-foot spurs.
- **Bays and estuaries**: shuffle your feet along the bottom rather than stepping — **stingrays** lie buried in shallow sand and their tail spike inflicts vicious wounds. Sea urchins cause pain and infection; wear footgear.
- **Do not handle** rabbitfish and tang or surgeonfish (venomous or scalpel-sharp fin spines), toadfish and weever fish (buried in sand, toxic dorsal spines), scorpion fish and the near-invisible stonefish (intensely painful stings).
- **Do not eat** puffer or blowfish (blood, liver and gonads lethally toxic), triggerfish, and tropical barracuda or large reef snappers, which may carry ciguatera. Never eat polar bear or bearded seal liver, or hawksbill turtle flesh.
- **Other sea hazards**: the blue-ringed octopus of Australia has a deadly bite — treat all tropical octopuses with caution; Portuguese men-of-war trail tentacles up to 12 meters (40 feet) that sting even from a washed-up, apparently dead animal; cone shells (ice-cream-cone shape) fire a venomous harpoon and must never be picked up, and the similar auger shells are nearly as dangerous.

> ⚠️ This guide is for avoidance and recognition, not harvest. When any plant or animal cannot be identified with certainty, the rule is simple: leave it alone.
